power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Obtaining accurate measures of changing abilities is essential for online adaptive learning systems (ALS) to provide learners with instructional material and practice items at the appropriate level.
Despite the large data volume in ALS, focusing on a single individual at a specific moment yields limited data, reducing measurement precision.
To improve precision, it has been proposed to incorporate response time (RT) data into measurement (Klinkenberg et al., 2011).
text.formatted: To improve precision, it has been proposed to incorporate response time (RT) data into measurement <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Klinkenberg et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Using data from an ALS for primary school mathematics Math Garden (Straatemeier, 2014), we compare different models that incorporate RTs and can be used for ability tracking with each other and with the benchmark Rasch model, in which ability is measured based only on the accuracy of the responses, in terms of next-response prediction.

We also contrast these empirical findings with simulation results that match the empirical setup but where the generating model matches the way in which RTs are incorporated into measurement, to study what can be gained under ideal circumstances.

Our results show that while theoretical gains are large, in the studied empirical setting RTs at best provide a modest improvement that was not fully consistent across domains and depended on the reward system implemented in the ALS.
Implications of the results for the choice of the measurement model in ALS are discussed.
Enhancing measurement in adaptive learning systems: How much can we gain from response times?

One of the most impactful and promising ambitions in educational innovation is the move toward large-scale personalized learning, facilitated by the emergence of online adaptive learning systems (ALS), also known as adaptive learning environments or computer adaptive practice systems (Ennouamani & Mahani, 2017).
text.formatted: One of the most impactful and promising ambitions in educational innovation is the move toward large-scale personalized learning, facilitated by the emergence of online adaptive learning systems (ALS), also known as adaptive learning environments or computer adaptive practice systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Ennouamani & Mahani, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These systems are designed to dynamically adjust the level of practice and instructional content according to each learner's abilities, as well as other potential characteristics such as learning preferences, interests, and motivation, fostering an engaging environment (Bernacki et al., 2021; Pelánek, 2025; Van Schoors et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These systems are designed to dynamically adjust the level of practice and instructional content according to each learner's abilities, as well as other potential characteristics such as learning preferences, interests, and motivation, fostering an engaging environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bernacki et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Pelánek, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Van Schoors et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Xie et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Examples of such systems include Franel, an item-based intelligent tutoring system for French and Dutch languages (Desmet et al., 2006), Outline Maps, an adaptive practice system for geography facts (Papoušek et al., 2016), and Math Garden, an online learning system for primary school mathematics (Straatemeier, 2014).
text.formatted: Examples of such systems include Franel, an item-based intelligent tutoring system for French and Dutch languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Desmet et al., 2006)</ref>, Outline Maps, an adaptive practice system for geography facts <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Papoušek et al., 2016)</ref>, and Math Garden, an online learning system for primary school mathematics <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Straatemeier, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Depending on the system, it can also provide diagnostic feedback, such as which skills and abilities the learner is deficient in, navigational support regarding which skills to work on, and learning resources for improving these skills.
To effectively optimize feedback, instruction, and educational materials, it is essential to have continuously updated, accurate, and reliable assessments of students' evolving abilities.
Consequently, measurement becomes a crucial aspect of ALS.

However, measuring change is inherently complex and the adaptive nature of ALS, combined with the necessity of serving thousands of learners who require ongoing updates to their ability estimates, adds further complexity.
These characteristics present significant challenges to traditional psychometric models and algorithms (see e.g., Deonovic et al., 2020; Wauters et al., 2012).
text.formatted: These characteristics present significant challenges to traditional psychometric models and algorithms (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Deonovic et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Wauters et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: To address these challenges, rating systems such as the Elo rating system (ERS; Elo, 1978) have been used to monitor abilities in ALS (Klinkenberg et al., 2011; Pelánek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To address these challenges, rating systems such as the Elo rating system (ERS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Elo, 1978)</ref> have been used to monitor abilities in ALS <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Klinkenberg et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Pelánek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In the ERS the students' abilities are updated based on every student-item interaction, based on the difference between the observed and expected response: where θjt and θj(t-1) are the estimates of ability of student j at timepoints t and t -1, respectively, and K is the step-size parameter.
Smaller K-values can be selected to reduce noise, while larger values allow to track changes better.
The expected response at timepoint t is calculated using the estimated ability at timepoint t -1 under the chosen measurement model.

A simple measurement model often used in this context is the Rasch model (RM; Rasch, 1960), in which the probability of a correct response only depends on the difference between ability of the student and the difficulty of the item.
text.formatted: A simple measurement model often used in this context is the Rasch model (RM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Rasch, 1960)</ref>, in which the probability of a correct response only depends on the difference between ability of the student and the difficulty of the item.

text.text: The difficulty of the items can either be updated alongside the abilities of the students, or fixed at pre-calibrated values.
The ERS provides a computationally efficient, easy-to-implement, and transparent way of tracking student abilities.

Nonetheless, a significant challenge persists: Despite the large volume of data generated by ALS, focusing on a specific individual at a given moment yields limited data, making it difficult to achieve high measurement precision using information from response accuracy alone.
Additionally, items with relatively high correct response probabilities (0.7-0.8) are typically selected to boost motivation and engagement (Jansen et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Additionally, items with relatively high correct response probabilities (0.7-0.8) are typically selected to boost motivation and engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Jansen et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the response accuracy data would provide less information about ability compared to settings where items are presented in the statistically optimal way with a probability of a correct response close to 0.5 (as is done in computerized adaptive testing aimed at optimizing test information in a personalized way; see e.g., van der Linden, Glas, et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Consequently, the response accuracy data would provide less information about ability compared to settings where items are presented in the statistically optimal way with a probability of a correct response close to 0.5 (as is done in computerized adaptive testing aimed at optimizing test information in a personalized way; see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">van der Linden, Glas, et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, selecting items that do not provide a lot of information makes the speed of convergence slower.

For example, in the cold-start problem, estimates of abilities move away from their initial values slower (Bolsinova et al., 2025), requiring a lot of responses before the estimates get close to their true values.
text.formatted: For example, in the cold-start problem, estimates of abilities move away from their initial values slower <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bolsinova et al., 2025)</ref>, requiring a lot of responses before the estimates get close to their true values.

text.text: Mismatches between the true ability level of the student and their estimated level of ability can therefore result in long periods for which the difficulty level of the presented items is not well-aligned with the ability level of student, causing issues for the ALS such as for example reducing student motivation, risk of dropout, and a slower learning rate due to presenting misaligned learning material.

In this study, we compare different models that incorporate RTs and can be used for monitoring ability with ERS (i.e., models based on scoring rules) with each other and with the benchmark RM in which ability is updated based only on accuracy data.
The logic for the setup is that if including RTs into the model improves measurement of ability, then it should increase prediction accuracy of next responses based on the ability estimates.

Since model misfit may introduce construct-irrelevant variance to the estimates, it is not a given that using the models with scoring rules that include RT as well as response accuracy will outperform the RM in terms of prediction accuracy, due to possibly introducing bias in the estimates that outweigh potential gains in precision.

Thus, we suggest to use prediction accuracy (rather than model-based assessments of precision of measurement) as the tool to assess whether including RTs into the scoring rule improves measurement in ALS, and to study which scoring rule seems to perform best in practice.
We use data from an online learning system called Math Garden for primary school mathematics, described in more detail in the Methods section.
The system has two interesting properties that make it an interesting case study.

First, gamification elements in the system focused on explicitly communicating the scoring rule to the students by showing the number of coins that they receive or lose based on the correctness of their response and the RT.
The measurement model corresponding to that communicated scoring rule, which we will refer to as the normative RT model, was used for item selection when the data were collected.

Second, a change in the scoring rule was made in 2019, moving from the SRTM to only differentiating the scores for correct responses based on RTs (Vermeiren et al., 2025), rather than for both correct and incorrect responses.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
First, we describe the online learning system and the datasets that we used in this study.
Second, we describe and motivate the scoring-rule-based models which we used.
Third, we describe the data analysis strategy.
Fourth, we present the results, describing the differences between the scoring rules on the different parts of the data.

Fifth, we present a simulation study, in which we mimic the conditions of the empirical example but generate data using the two normative models used in Math Garden, in order to study the improvements in measurement under ideal conditions.
Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the choice of a measurement model in ALS.

text.text: The idea behind working with dichotomized RT instead of continuous RT is that the linearity assumptions for the relationship between RTs and ability made by the SRTM may be too restrictive in some settings.
The DSRTM is less restrictive, while still retaining the idea of giving higher credit/penalty to fast responses than to slow responses.

When working with ERSs, one has to decide whether the item difficulties are updated alongside the abilities of the students, or whether precalibrated values will be used for the item difficulties that are not updated alongside ability.

While updating the item difficulties has the benefit of tracking changes over time in the item parameters, an important downside in adaptive settings is that it also introduces variance inflation (Bolsinova et al., 2025; Hofman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: While updating the item difficulties has the benefit of tracking changes over time in the item parameters, an important downside in adaptive settings is that it also introduces variance inflation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bolsinova et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Hofman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: That is, the variance of the estimates of ability across students artificially increases over time if item difficulties are updated.

While it has been shown that this issue can be avoided by using parallel chains of estimates (Bolsinova et al., 2025), this is something that needs to be implemented during data collection and cannot be applied retroactively.

text.text: Thus, when using existing data that were collected adaptively without such an implementation, updating item difficulties together with student abilities would lead to variance inflation.
Moreover, such variance inflation may be affecting different models to a different extent and hence would jeopardize our objective of comparing the performance of the different models.
Therefore, to ensure comparability of the models, we use the ERS with item parameters fixed at calibrated values, and a calibration step was needed.

In this step, the item parameters for each of the models were estimated using the calibration dataset and then fixed to these estimates when running the Elo algorithm to dynamically measure the ability of the students in the training and testing datasets in Steps 2 and 3.
In this step, the objective is solely to obtain estimates for the item parameters based on a calibration data set, to be used in the later two steps.
While the focus is on estimating the item parameters, this cannot be done without also modeling ability of the students.
On the one hand, fitting a measurement model to a calibration dataset that would fully ignore the change in abilities over time can be expected to lead to some degree of bias in the item parameters.
On the other hand, implementing a full dynamic model to account for change within and between sessions would not be computationally feasible, and exceed the purpose of this calibration step.
With these considerations in mind, we opted to allow student ability to change across sessions, without explicitly modeling growth.
To achieve this, we divided the data of each person into separate sessions (items answered within one day) and treated each of these sessions as if they came from separate respondents.

For simplicity, the data of different 'pseudo-respondents' originating from the same student were treated as though they were independent (i.e., dependence between the different sessions of a student was ignored), and the full set of pseudo-respondents were taken to come from a single population distribution, allowing marginal maximum likelihood estimation (Bock & Aitkin, 1981) to be applied.

text.text: To evaluate the practical significance the MSE differences found in the empirical data we performed a simulation study (see next section).
Overall, RT-based models performed best in the Addition and Subtraction domains when the old scoring rule was used.
Here, the SRTM, the PCM, and the NRM performed better than the RM, consistently across the twelve data splits.
When the new scoring rule was introduced, the NRM was the only RT-based model that had lower MSE than the RM in three of the domains.

For the Division domain when the new scoring rule was used, the RM and the NRM performed similarly, with one model performing better in some data splits and another in others (i.e., the range of MSE differences covers both negative and positive values).
In all datasets the best performing RT-based model was the NRM.

It is the model that makes the least assumptions about the relationship between RT and ability: It only uses RTs of correct responses in its scoring rule, does not assume linearity in the relationship between RT and ability, and does not assume that only one item parameter is sufficient to describe both the accuracy and RT aspects of item performance.

The score for incorrect responses in the NRM ranged from -4 to -1 in the different datasets (the scores were less negative in datasets with a larger difference between the NRM and the benchmark RM; for the optimized values across datasets see Appendix C).

The score for the incorrect responses was always lower in the NRM than in the PCM, meaning that the NRM gives relatively less weight to the RTs (i.e., the distance between the scores of correct and incorrect responses were much larger than the differences between the scores for fast and slow correct responses).
Interestingly, the CRTM with the small penalty for incorrect responses was one of the worst models in all datasets, even though it was the normative model when the new scoring rule was used.
This is not surprising if we look at the correlations between the ability estimates under the different models.

We computed the correlations between the expected a posteriori estimates of ability in Step 1 of the analysis for each of the RT-based models on the one hand and the RM on the other (i.e., ability measure reflecting only accuracy).
The correlations for the CRTM P = 0.1 ranged between .868 and .924 in the different datasets, while for the best performing NRM they were .977-.998.

That is, for these datasets the ability measure obtained under the CRTM with a small penalty deviated notably from those obtained under the RM, and this difference was much larger than for any of the other RT-based models.

This can be explained by considering that the CRTM with P = 0.1 gives a relatively high weight to being fast vs. slow in its scoring rule, compared to the difference between giving a correct and an incorrect response.

That is, the difference in score between a fast and a slow correct response can be as large as 1, while the difference between a (slow) correct response and an incorrect response can be as small as 0.1.

Thus, the ability measure of the CRTM much more than that of the other models tends to reflect individual differences in speededness than in ability to produce correct responses, and in settings where speed is not only determined by ability but also by other factors (e.g., risk-taking of the student or student self-confidence) one can expect this ability measure to deviate the most from that of the RM.

The DSRTM which was introduced as a way of relaxing the assumption of the linear relationship between ability and RT present in the SRTM performed worse than the RM across datasets, and in some datasets worse than all other models.
That is, we did not find added value of moving from continuous to discrete scores within the signed-residual time scoring rule.
However, further relaxing the model by including extra item parameters (PCM) leads to better prediction compared to both the RM and the SRTM in some of the datasets.
Importantly, the NRM is the only model that did not deteriorate next-response prediction across all datasets.

All other models are showing results worse than the benchmark in at least some datasets, with the increase of MSE compared to the RM often being much larger (e.g., +.00202 for the SRTM in the Division domain when the old scoring rule was used) than the decrease (-.00008 for the SRTM in the Addition domain when the old scoring rule was used), which underscores the importance of evaluating the effects of adding RTs on prediction accuracy.

Because it is not a given that the potential added value of using RTs is stable as the number of responses increases, we also specifically considered the performance of the RT-based models in terms of their prediction accuracy gains and losses compared to the benchmark RM for observations binned based on the number of responses up to that point.

The MSEs were calculated based on the observations that fell specifically into that bin (i.e., in the first bin the MSE was calculated using only the first five responses, and in the second bin using only responses six through ten).
Note that the last bin no longer includes all students which may introduce confounding in the comparison.

Therefore, we focus on the first four bins (1-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20) which allows us to evaluate how the models compare during the cold start where one may expect that considering additional information from RTs may provide the most benefit.

To investigate how the results in the empirical data compare to what one can expect in terms of improvement of measurement in the best case scenario, that is when the normative RT model is the data generating model, we performed a simulation study.
For each empirical dataset we generated simulated datasets that would mimic its structure.
We kept the same number of responses and the same items that each student received in the empirical data.

The response accuracy and RT data were generated under the SRTM for the datasets with the old scoring rule and under the CRTM with a small penalty (P = 0.1) for the datasets with the new scoring rule.
Additionally, we considered a scenario in which the RTs do not follow the normative models and provide no information about ability.
In this scenario we re-sampled RT values with replacement from the empirical distributions specific to each item and conditional on response accuracy.

This allowed to create simulated data where the RT distributions and the relationships between RT and accuracy are the same as in the empirical data, but RTs are not expected to improve measurement of ability.
To specify the true values of the item parameters we used the estimates of the item parameters under the RM averaged across data splits.

These values were used to generate data under the SRTM (i.e., under the normative model in the old scoring rule datasets) and to generate response accuracy under the RM in the scenario with random RTs.
To specify the corresponding true values for the item parameters in the CRTM with P = 0.1, the values from the RM needed to go through a non-linear transformation 11.
For each student we aimed to obtain a rough approximation of their learning curve in the empirical data and use that as their true learning curve for the simulation.
We used the Elo algorithm with our benchmark RM to do that.
The optimal K-values from the empirical data were used.

Models that make use of RT-based scoring rules have the potential to improve quality of measurement in ALS over what can be achieved using response-accuracy-only models such as the RM.

In this research, we focused on prediction accuracy as one of the aspects of measurement quality and studied both the empirical and theoretical gains that can be obtained using different RT-based models, with both the empirical and simulation-based analysis considered in the context of a case study ALS in mathematics for elementary school students.

Both the empirical and simulation-based results suggest potential for improving the measurement quality, as evaluated by the accuracy with which next responses can be predicted based on the current ability estimate under each of the different models.

However, the simulation-based results show a much more positive picture than was observed in the empirical setting, where the gains in measurement were somewhat small and not fully consistent, and where the normative models did not notably outperform the benchmark model that made use of response accuracy only.
While there was some improvement in the MSE when using some of the RT-based models instead of the RM in some of the datasets, the improvement over the benchmark in those cases was rather small.

When we compared it to the improvement in simulated data, we observed that the largest improvement in the empirical data roughly matched what can be expected if there were 10% more responses available.
The achieved improvement, although non-negligible, is not large and does not hold universally across datasets.

The notable difference between the observed gains when studying the empirical data versus when studying simulated data obtained under the normative models comes from notable differences between the relationship between RT and ability as specified by the models versus what happens in reality, which can be considered problematic for the interpretation of scores produced under these models.
When the ability and RTs are not as strongly related to each other compared to what the normative model assumes, the empirical gains of including RTs are notably smaller.

And when the assumed relationship is largely absent in the data or when it is in the different direction from what is observed in the empirical data, using a normative model leads to the decrease of prediction accuracy compared to the benchmark.
These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating the assumptions of RT-based models in empirical data.
Both the SRTM and the CRTM have been designed with the idea that explicitly communicating the RT-based scoring rule to the respondents should lead to them behaving according to that model.
Analyzing the data from an online learning environment where these scoring rules have been implemented, we found that this is not necessarily the case.

The normative models were not the best performing models in our study, nor did they provide notable improvements in measurement over using the RM, while in some datasets notably increasing prediction error.

These results emphasize that when implementing a measurement model which takes RTs into account it is important to check whether its theoretical expectations match the empirical relationships in the data.
More specifically, studying the relationship between ability and RTs of correct and incorrect responses is a crucial step in choosing a measurement model for the system.

Our results also show that changing the instructions for respondents (here, changing the rewards/penalties within the system communicated to the students) may change the relationship between ability and RTs, and may also affect whether RT-based models are beneficial for measurement.

In this case, making the penalty for incorrect responses independent of RT made RTs of correct responses less informative about ability, as evidenced by the correlation between the RT of correct responses and ability shifting further away from where the normative model predicts it to be.
Findings such as these strongly suggest that any changes in the instructions or the reward system in the game should be followed by a new evaluation of the measurement models.
Interestingly enough, the RT-based model that showed the best performance in the empirical setting was the NRM.
This model has to our knowledge not yet been considered in the context of utilizing RTs in ALS, but it outperformed both the normative models and the other considered models.
It is likely that its better performance can to some extent be attributed to it also being the most flexible model of the set.

It should be noted that this may suggest that the degree of misspecification present in the other models is likely their main obstacle to showing good performance in the empirical setting, as was also evidenced by the large contrast between the theoretical gains (studied through simulation) versus the empirical gains obtained for the two normative models.

It is quite plausible that a model that is more specific than that NRM but that also more closely matches the actual response process than the models considered in this research could also outperform the NRM.
However, what this model would need to look like needs to be a topic of further research, and would likely require a more in-depth study of the response behavior of students in the ALS.
It is however clear that because it outperformed all other models, future studies in this direction should definitely consider including the NRM as one of the benchmark models.
A notable limitation of the current study is the assymetry between the compared models: First, the item sequences presented to students were determined based on the normative model.

Second, the instructions to the students were aligned with this model (note, that while in Math Garden the scoring rule of the normative model is explicitely communicated to the students, in general the model used for abiltiy estimation and item selection does not have to be aligned with the scoring rule communicated to the student).
The counterfactual data (e.g., items selected based on the RM and/or students not instructed to pay attention their response times) are not available.

Since we have observed that when instructions changed from the old to the new scoring rule, student behavior and relationships between ability and response times have changed, we can also expect that if the scoring rule from the RM were communicated to the students, their behavior would be different as well, and therefore the consequences of incorporating RTs for prediction accuracy could be different.
The assymetry in terms of the which model was used for item selection is less crucial.

Previous simulation studies (Niznan et al., 2015) showed that while the magnitude of differences between the models depends on the model used for item selection (the better the model used for item selection is, the closer the probabilities-correct of the selected items are to the target probabilities, the smaller the difference between the different models become), the model closest to the data generating model still provides better estimates of ability and higher prediction accuracy.

text.text: The starting point of this study has been that RTs are incorporated into the measurement model to increase precision of measurement, without altering the measurement itself.

That is, we assume that ability measured by accuracy only is a valid measure, but that in standard ALS settings the precision of the accuracy-based measure is low due to data sparsity and item selection aimed at optimised student engagement rather than statistical information in the responses.
From this perspective it makes sense to use prediction of the accuracy of the next response as the criterion for model comparison and for contrasting the RM with each of the RT-based models.

However, a different perspective that could be taken is that an accuracy-based ability measure is not necessarily the best measure of ability (e.g., one may argue that to be good at addition one needs to not only be correct but also demonstrate fluency), and that incorporating RTs is not just a way to increase precision, but a way of changing the operationalization of the construct and potentially improving validity of score interpretations.

From this perspective, misalignment of accuracy and RT information within RT-based models would not necessarily be taken as a reason to not use the model, but rather as a sign that the resulting measure of ability is a composite score of the accuracy and RT components, which are not perfectly aligned with each other.

However, to make such an argument, one would need to provide evidence of increased validity of these alternative interpretations, for example by comparing the ability estimates form different models with student grades or with scores from standardized assessments, as a way of evaluating external validity.

Since differences in RTs may reflect not only construct-relevant variance (i.e., reflect higher mastery of skills that require fluency and automatization) but also carry construct-irrelevant variance (e.g., reading speed, motor speed, familiarity with computerised practice, rapid guessing), the alternative operationalization should not be taken as a better measure of ability without such evidence.

Regardless of the answer to the question about the best operationalization of ability, increasing prediction error for the accuracy of the next response after incorporation of RTs in the model is an important problem within an ALS.

When prediction is less accurate, selected items would be less closely matching the desired level of accuracy, which is often used as a criterion for item selection (e.g., in Math Garden students choose a difficulty level with either 60%, 75% or 90% expected correct responses), which can lead to either an over-or an under-challenging environment for some students.
An undesired consequence of that could be that students from specific groups would be disadvantaged.
One possibility concerns gender differences in response behavior.
For example, research often shows that girls are more cautious than boys (Jansen et al., 2016).

text.text: If such differences occur, girls' ability would be underestimated and boys' abilities overestimated if RTs of correct responses are taken into account, and as a result item selection would unintentionally result in presenting more difficult items to boys than to girls, given the same ability level of the student.
It was not possible to examine this gender-related implication as part of the current study because information on gender was not available.
It therefore represents a conjecture that warrants further investigation.
In this study we compared data from a natural experiment consisting of two periods, during which different scoring rules were implemented in Math Garden.

It is important to note however that while the change in the scoring rule was the main change introduced in the system, it is not the only thing that was different between the academic years of 2018-2019 and 2020-2021, which is a limitation of the current study.
For example, new domains have been added to the system and new ways of recommending different domains within the system to students were introduced (Brinkhuis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, new domains have been added to the system and new ways of recommending different domains within the system to students were introduced <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brinkhuis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The consequences of this can be noticed in there being fewer students and fewer responses per student in the 2020-2021 dataset, since some students who would have otherwise been practicing in the four domains included in this study chose other domains to practice.

Potentially the composition of the population of the students practicing in our four domains in 2020-2021 could be different compared to that from 2018-2019, which could also be contributing to the differences in response behavior that we found.
Furthermore, there may be other differences between the two time periods included in the study, for example in terms of increased digitalisation at schools (also due to the COVID-19 pandemic).
RT patterns may have changed if the students became more used to working with digital platforms or if the dominant type of devices used for practice changed.
Detailed study of potential mode effects goes beyond the scope of the current paper but is an important direction for further research.
All RT-based models included in this study assume that the same relationship between ability and RTs holds for all students.
As such, these models do not take into account any individual differences in response behavior that go beyond the differences in ability.
However, some students might be generally faster than others with the same ability level.
Failing to account for these differences may be one of the reasons that the models do not provide a lot of improvement over the benchmark RM.

Additionally, the environment allowed students to choose their desired difficulty level (operationalized through the expected proportion correct), and there may be relevant differences between students who choose a relatively easy versus hard difficulty level, which could also potentially have had an impact on the results.
Developing ways of taking all of these individual differences into account could lead to better models, which would improve measurement precision without introducing confounding.
Future research should also focus on studying the differences between people from different subgroups (e.g., gender, language spoken at home).

While for the standard ERS the underlying measurement model is the RM, where ability is measured based on binary item scores (1 -correct, 0 -incorrect), in this modified ERS the signed-residual-time model (SRTM; Maris & van der Maas, 2012) is used which incorporates RTs in the item scores.

text.text: The idea of this RT-based score is that RTs provide information about ability beyond what is captured by response accuracy alone: Correct responses still indicate a higher ability level than incorrect responses, but the speed with which that response was provided additionally influences the indicated ability level, and the way in which RTs relate to ability depends on response accuracy.
Concretely, it is assumed that responses that are both correct and fast indicate higher ability compared to responses that are correct yet slow.
The converse is assumed for incorrect responses, where fast incorrect responses are taken to indicate a lower ability level than slow incorrect responses.
Note that these assumptions are not guaranteed to hold universally as RTs are influenced by many different factors.
